significance.justification: Verified true, the claim would establish that, for successful encoded jailbreaks, “decoding lags the refusal decision” and that a “late-layer refusal re-check” causally restores refusal; this is a form-(iii) ordering between measurable computations coupled to a form-(ii) intervention, establishing both the behavioral phenomenon and a specific timing mechanism. CipherChat (Yuan et al., ICLR 2024) documents safety failures under encoded interaction, while Arditi et al., “Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction” (NeurIPS 2024), makes the timing of refusal-related representations consequential: the proposed ordering would constrain explanations of which encoded attacks should succeed and whether safety checks must recur after semantic decoding. The claim is determinate, and a negative result would rule out refusal-before-decode as the general explanation, though not broader capability–safety mismatch accounts; after topic substitution, generic mechanistic LLM safety would not earn this score, because the specific cross-layer ordering is what raises it above the topic median.

reach.justification: The named handle is a “late-layer refusal re-check” reading the “post-decode representation,” an ex-ante inference-time intervention that can block harmful output after intent becomes legible but before the model completes its answer. After per-model re-extraction, the claim predicts a transferable relation—decoding should occur later than the decisive refusal computation on successful cipher attacks—rather than merely supplying an open-ended probe, although the admitted “model-dependent layer structure” limits transfer of absolute layers and directions. Its asserted scope covers Base64, ciphers, and leetspeak, and the downstream users could include model auditors and deployers implementing a decode-aware safety gate; the topic-substitution check lowers no further because that concrete preventive handle and temporal relation, not generic LLM safety, support the score.
